video_metadata.working_title: ARIZONA 1992 Cold Case Solved After 22 Years — Justice for Angela Brosso and Melanie Bernas
video_metadata.topic_one_sentence: Two young women were killed while riding their bikes along the Arizona Canal in north Phoenix in November 1992 and September 1993; the case stayed unsolved for 22 years until a Y-DNA surname search in public genealogy databases and a covertly collected DNA sample led to the January 2015 arrest of Bryan Patrick Miller, a Phoenix man known locally as the costumed 'Zombie Hunter', who was convicted in April 2023 and sentenced to death in June 2023.
video_metadata.primary_emotion_to_evoke: grief turning into quiet vindication; unease at how ordinary and visible the killer was

protagonist._instructions: The main character of your story - can be hero, villain, or antihero. Fill with verified facts only.
protagonist.age_at_time_of_events: About 20 in November 1992 and about 21 in September 1993 (derived: 42 at his January 2015 arrest, 50 at his June 2023 sentencing). Exact birth date not verified.
protagonist.occupation_or_status: Phoenix resident; at the time of arrest he lived in the Sunnyslope neighborhood of Phoenix with his daughter. Convicted in April 2023; sentenced to death June 7, 2023; on Arizona death row.
protagonist.location: Phoenix, Arizona; lived for a period in Everett, Washington, after the murders.
protagonist.physical_description: Not used in the script beyond public photos; no description verified.
protagonist.background_brief: At about 16, in 1989, he stabbed a woman in the back in the parking lot of Paradise Valley Mall in Phoenix and served about a year in juvenile detention; the victim testified at his 2022 trial. A few years after the canal murders he moved to Everett, Washington, where he was charged with assault in 2002 and reportedly acquitted. He later moved back to Phoenix with his daughter into a home that had belonged to a grandmother, described by police as a hoarding situation.
protagonist.psychological_profile: At trial the defense argued he was insane at the time of the murders because of autism and dissociative disorders rooted in severe childhood abuse by his mother; the judge rejected insanity and convicted him. At sentencing the judge accepted that the childhood abuse was proven as mitigation but imposed death. He has maintained he did not commit the murders.
protagonist.mundane_humanizing_detail: He was known in Phoenix's science-fiction and comic convention scene as the 'Zombie Hunter', a costumed character he played in public.

victims_or_targets._instructions: People affected by the protagonist's actions. Include 3-5 key figures minimum.

individuals.name: Angela 'Angie' Brosso
individuals.role_or_profession: 21-year-old who worked at a Phoenix technology firm on a new interactive voice response system; had studied at the DeVry Institute of Technology in Los Angeles; grew up in Camp Hill, Pennsylvania; moved to Phoenix in June 1992 with her boyfriend.
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Killed on the night of November 8, 1992, on the eve of her 22nd birthday, while on a solo evening bike ride near her apartment and the Arizona Canal in north Phoenix. Her body was found the next morning; part of her remains was recovered from the canal about ten days later by a man who was fishing.
individuals.humanizing_detail: Her boyfriend stayed home that night to bake her a birthday cake. A former boss and co-worker described her as bold, someone who would always make you laugh or smile; she enjoyed riding her bike.

individuals.name: Melanie Bernas [MINOR, 17]
individuals.role_or_profession: 17-year-old junior at Arcadia High School in Phoenix who had signed up for accelerated classes.
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Went out on an evening bike ride on September 21, 1993, while her mother was at dinner; she was stabbed and found dead in the Arizona Canal on the morning of September 22, 1993, about a mile and a half from where Angela Brosso had been found.
individuals.humanizing_detail: Friends described her as adventurous and spontaneous (azfamily, May 18, 2023).

individuals.name: The 1989 Paradise Valley Mall stabbing survivor (name not used)
individuals.role_or_profession: Woman attacked in a mall parking lot in Phoenix in 1989.
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: Stranger stabbed by Miller when he was about 16.
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Stabbed in the back; survived; testified at the 2022 trial, 33 years later.
individuals.humanizing_detail: Her testimony let the court hear about the attack decades later.

collective_victims_if_applicable.group_description: Families of Angela and Melanie, and the cyclists, runners and residents who used the north Phoenix canal paths.
collective_victims_if_applicable.total_number_affected: Two murder victims; one earlier stabbing survivor.
collective_victims_if_applicable.range_of_impacts: Decades of grief, fear on the canal paths, and a 22-year wait for an arrest followed by more than eight years to a sentence.

chronological_timeline._instructions: List every significant event with exact dates when possible. This is the backbone of your script.

events.what_happened: The Arizona Canal, the northernmost of the Salt River Valley's main irrigation canals, was built in the 1880s; by the 1990s its banks were used as paths by cyclists and runners.
events.source: General historical background (Salt River Project history); verify exact year

events.location: Paradise Valley Mall parking lot, Phoenix
events.what_happened: Miller, then about 16, stabbed a woman in the back; he served about one year in juvenile detention.
Angela Brosso moved to Phoenix and rented an apartment with her boyfriend.
Presidential election; Arizona voters also approved a Martin Luther King Jr. holiday.

events.location: North Phoenix, near the Arizona Canal (Cactus Road / Interstate 17 area per one source)
events.what_happened: Angela Brosso, 21, went on a solo evening bike ride on the eve of her 22nd birthday; her boyfriend stayed home baking her birthday cake. When she did not return, he searched three times on his bike and then reported her missing.
events.source: CBS News 48 Hours timeline; azfamily Oct 5, 2022

events.location: Near a bike path by the canal, north Phoenix
events.what_happened: Angela's body was found the next morning.
events.source: CBS News 48 Hours timeline; KOLD/azfamily Sept 29, 2022

events.what_happened: About ten days later, part of her remains was found in the canal by a man who was fishing.

Melanie Bernas, 17, an Arcadia High School junior, went for an evening bike ride while her mother was out to dinner (left just after 7 p.m.). Her mother came home to find Melanie and her bike gone and called emergency rooms.
events.source: Arizona Republic via Yahoo News (mother's testimony); CBS News

events.location: Arizona Canal, about 1.5 miles from the Brosso site
events.what_happened: Melanie was found dead in the canal; she had been stabbed.
events.significance: Discovery; DNA later linked both cases
events.source: Arizona Republic via Yahoo; Oxygen; CBS News

events.what_happened: DNA evidence collected after both crimes showed the attacks were linked to the same unknown man.
Miller moved to Everett, Washington, a few years after the murders.
Miller was charged with assault in an attack on a woman, who survived; he was reportedly acquitted.
Miller moved back to Phoenix with his daughter into a home that had belonged to a grandmother.
events.significance: Killer living in the city where the crimes occurred

events.what_happened: Forensic genealogist Colleen Fitzpatrick approached Phoenix police at a conference and ran the crime-scene Y-DNA profile against public genealogy databases; the result pointed to the surname Miller.
Detectives narrowed a list including men named Miller; undercover officers took Bryan Patrick Miller to lunch at a restaurant and collected his DNA from a glass.
events.source: CBS News; azfamily trial coverage; ABC15

events.what_happened: The covert sample matched the crime-scene DNA; Miller, 42, was arrested at his home and charged in both murders.
events.source: CBS News 48 Hours timeline; 12News; Fox News

events.what_happened: Miller pleaded not guilty.
Years of delay over mental health and an insanity defense; a judge found him competent to stand trial; Miller waived a jury.
events.source: Court TV (mentally fit); Oxygen (insanity defense); AP

events.what_happened: Bench trial began before Judge Suzanne Cohen; Angela's boyfriend, Melanie's mother, retired detective Mike Meislish and the 1989 stabbing survivor testified; the 2015 interrogation video was shown.
events.source: KOLD/azfamily Sept 29, 2022; azfamily Oct 5, Oct 6, Oct 12, Nov 3, 2022; Yahoo/Arizona Republic

events.what_happened: Judge Cohen found Miller guilty on all counts: two counts each of first-degree murder, kidnapping and attempted sexual assault (AP wording), rejecting the insanity defense.
Penalty phase: Angela's mother and Melanie's sister testified.
Miller spoke, saying he was not seeking sympathy and hoped the families could find peace.

events.location: Maricopa County Superior Court, downtown Phoenix
events.what_happened: Judge Cohen sentenced Miller, 50, to death for each murder, plus prison terms on the other counts (24 years reported).
events.source: azfamily June 7, 2023; Fox 10; Court TV; Maricopa County Attorney's Office

events.what_happened: In interviews for 48 Hours / azfamily, Miller said death row is cold and the food 'not great' and denied committing the murders.

Automatic appeal CR-23-0157-AP: opening-brief deadline extended to June 12, 2024, then to September 10, 2024, with a warning that no further extensions would be granted absent extraordinary circumstances.
No ruling on the automatic appeal was found in research; Miller remains under sentence of death.
events.source: Searches of news and docket, Oct 2026

cold_open_material._instructions: The most dramatic moment of your story - this will be your hook.

the_moment.exact_location: North Phoenix, Arizona, near the Arizona Canal
the_moment.what_is_happening: Angela Brosso leaves for a solo evening bike ride on the eve of her 22nd birthday while her boyfriend stays home to bake her birthday cake.
the_moment.what_makes_it_shocking: She never comes home; ten months later a 17-year-old high school junior on her own evening bike ride along the same canal is killed about a mile and a half away; the same DNA is left behind.
the_moment.ironic_twist: The man the DNA finally named in 2015 was a familiar figure in Phoenix fan conventions, playing a costumed hero called the 'Zombie Hunter', living in the same city.

cold_open_material.central_mystery_question: Who was riding the dark canal paths of north Phoenix in 1992 and 1993, and how did a surname hidden in a hobby genealogy database lead to him 22 years later?

the_method._instructions: Technical details that can be explained to a general audience.
the_method.technique_name: Y-chromosome STR surname search in public genetic genealogy databases (an early form of forensic genetic genealogy), followed by covert reference DNA collection
step_by_step_explanation: Crime-scene DNA from both cases came from the same unknown man; his profile never matched anyone in criminal DNA databases.
The Y chromosome is passed from father to son almost unchanged, much like a surname in many families.
Genealogy hobbyists upload Y-DNA marker results to public databases, often listed with their surnames.
Colleen Fitzpatrick entered the crime-scene Y-DNA marker numbers into her software and searched the public databases; the closest matches carried the surname Miller.
This did not identify anyone; it suggested the killer was likely related through the male line to men named Miller.
Phoenix detectives compared the surname with their list of persons of interest and narrowed it to a handful of men.
Undercover officers took Bryan Patrick Miller to lunch and collected the glass he drank from.
The laboratory compared his DNA with the crime-scene profile and found a match on January 13, 2015.
the_method.why_it_worked: Male-line DNA and surnames often travel together; combined with an existing suspect list, the surname turned thousands of possibilities into a few.

technical_terms_to_explain.simple_explanation: A set of short repeated DNA patterns on the Y chromosome, passed from father to son like a family name.
The FBI-run network of criminal DNA databases; national searching began in 1998.
DNA left on an object a person throws away or leaves behind, such as a glass, which police can collect without a warrant under U.S. law in most situations.

the_method.scale_of_operation: Suspect pool reportedly narrowed from a long list to about five or six men named Miller (sources differ).

systemic_failure._instructions: What institution, system, or authority failed to prevent this?
systemic_failure.institution_that_failed: No single institution; the limits of early-1990s DNA databases and of the justice system's handling of a teenager who had already stabbed a stranger.
systemic_failure.how_they_were_supposed_to_protect: A prior violent offender's DNA in a database could have produced a match.
systemic_failure.why_they_failed: In 1992-1993 there was no national DNA database; Miller's 1989 offense was handled in juvenile court; the 2002 Washington case reportedly ended in acquittal.
specific_incompetence_examples: 1989 stabbing: about one year in juvenile detention (azfamily).
22 years between the first murder and the arrest; more than 8 more years to a sentence.
systemic_failure.ironic_details_about_the_failure: The killer lived openly in Phoenix, appeared in costume at public fan events, and was matched only after a private genealogist offered help at a conference.

the_investigation.investigating_agency: Phoenix Police Department (homicide and cold case units); Maricopa County Attorney's Office
the_investigation.initial_wrong_assumptions: Not documented in our sources; not used in the script.
the_investigation.the_fatal_mistake: Accepting a lunch invitation from undercover officers and leaving his glass behind.
the_investigation.how_long_until_caught: About 22 years and 2 months after the first murder.

the_confrontation._instructions: The arrest, raid, or climactic moment when everything collapses.
the_confrontation.scene_description: Arrested at home after the DNA match; interrogated the same day; the interrogation video was shown at trial in November 2022.
the_confrontation.protagonist_reaction: Pleaded not guilty on February 2, 2015; later pursued an insanity defense; maintains he did not commit the murders.
the_confrontation.ironic_or_absurd_details: The home was described by police as a hoarding situation.

charges_filed: Sexual assault-related counts (AP: two counts of attempted sexual assault; some outlets describe one sexual assault and one attempted sexual assault)
legal_resolution.trial_date_if_applicable: Bench trial began in early October 2022 before Judge Suzanne Cohen; verdict April 11, 2023.
legal_resolution.notable_court_testimony: Angela's boyfriend described her last day; Marlene Bernas testified by phone; retired detective Mike Meislish described the Bernas scene; the 1989 stabbing survivor testified; the defense argued insanity based on autism, dissociative disorders and childhood abuse.
legal_resolution.sentence_received: Death, imposed June 7, 2023, for each first-degree murder, plus prison terms on the remaining counts.
legal_resolution.protagonist_statement_in_court: May 22, 2023: said he was not seeking sympathy and hoped the families could find peace (paraphrase).
legal_resolution.current_status: As of October 2026: on Arizona death row; automatic appeal to the Arizona Supreme Court (CR-23-0157-AP) — no decision found in research. Re-verify before publishing.

universal_stakes.why_this_matters_to_viewer: Two young women doing something ordinary, riding a bike in their own neighborhood, were killed by a stranger.
universal_stakes.how_this_could_happen_to_them: Shared public paths; a familiar face in the community.
universal_stakes.lesson_or_warning: DNA preserved carefully in 1992 waited 22 years for the science to catch up; consumer genealogy has changed what is possible and raised privacy questions.
universal_stakes.current_relevance: One of the earliest uses of public genealogy databases by U.S. police, three years before the Golden State Killer arrest.
